Cynicism. This is an ancient Greek school of philosophy founded by Antisthenes and exemplified by Diogenes of Sinope. It teaches that virtue is the highest good and achieved through the renunciation of worldly desires, social conventions, and physical comfort. Unlike Stoicism, which accepts social duty and reason-based participation in civic life, Cynics rejected society itself as corrupt and artificial. They advocated instead a radical asceticism and provocative mockery of conventional values. The Cynic sage lives simply, often in public transgression of social norms, to expose the arbitrary and constraining nature of custom and to liberate the mind from false desires. Though the movement declined in antiquity, Cynicism reappeared in the Enlightenment and remains a strand in modern anti-establishment thought.

Antisthenes, who lived around 445 to 365 BCE, founded Cynicism. He was a student of Socrates. Diogenes of Sinope, living around 404 to 323 BCE, became the movement's most famous exemplar. He famously lived in a barrel and defied authority and decorum. Cynics taught that virtue is the only true good, but they defined virtue as freedom from desire and independence. Comfort, wealth, reputation, and even family are impediments to freedom and virtue.

The Cynic path requires askesis, a Greek word meaning training or discipline—not to achieve transcendence but to strip away the false needs society has imposed. A Cynic eats the cheapest food, wears rags, and scorns luxury. Cynics employed parrhesia, or bold speech, and transgressive public acts to shock people into seeing through social illusions. This is why cynicism in the modern sense means skepticism of professed motives and conventional morality.

Unlike Stoics, Cynics rejected civic participation, law, and justice as invented fictions. The Cynic wise person has no loyalty to the state or its laws, only to virtue and freedom. Diogenes is remembered for extreme acts: allegedly living in a tub, masturbating in the agora, instructing people to tread on his pride, and famously telling Alexander the Great to get out of his light. Cynic ideas influenced later Christian monasticism, particularly its asceticism and renunciation, and influenced modern critiques of capitalism and consumerism. The Cynic vision of freedom through renunciation continues to challenge materialistic societies.
